content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidance in 2019 on conducting intra-action reviews for COVID-19 responses. This document emphasizes the importance of identifying key dates during public health events to improve outbreak detection and response. Below are the key points explained in professional terms: 1. Date of Emergence: The date of emergence refers to when a health event is first detected. Often, this date is initially unknown and must be determined retrospectively using epidemiological data collected during outbreak investigations. As more information becomes available, including earlier cases, the date of emergence may be revised. For non-endemic diseases, this is typically the date when the index case or the first epidemiologically linked case experienced symptoms. For other health threats, it is the date when the event met the criteria for a reportable event based on current reporting standards. For example, in malaria outbreaks, the date of emergence is the last day of the epidemiological week when cases exceeded the alert threshold. 2. Date of Detection: The date of detection is the first date when a public health event is recorded in any system or by any source. This could be through a case investigation form, laboratory requisition form, clinical chart, or even media reports. For example, in a measles outbreak, if a local newspaper reports a cluster of deaths among children, and this is picked up by an event-based surveillance analyst, the date of detection is when the analyst records the event. 3. Date of Notification: The date of notification is when the event is first reported to a public health authority responsible for taking action. In countries with multi-level reporting systems, the earliest date any public health authority is notified is considered the notification date. For example, in the case of Ebola virus disease, if a clinician contacts a public health department about a suspected case, this is the notification date. If the case is detected through laboratory results without prior reporting, the notification date is when the public health authority receives the lab results. 4. Date Early Response Actions Are Completed: The 7-1-7 approach identifies seven early response actions that should be completed within seven days of notification. The date of completion is the latest date on which any of these actions is finalized. If some actions are not applicable, the latest date among the applicable actions is used. For example, early response actions may include activating an incident management system, initiating risk communication, or drafting an incident action plan. The aim is to initiate the response within one day of notification to minimize delays. 5. Early Response Initiation: While not used to calculate the 7-1-7 metrics, the date of early response initiation (when the first of the seven early response actions is completed) is critical for identifying bottlenecks in response initiation. The goal is to begin early response actions promptly, ideally within one day of notification. 6. Guidance for Improvement: WHO recommends using these dates to monitor and improve outbreak detection and response. Expanding early response actions into disease-specific job aids can enhance performance and accountability. This guidance is part of WHO’s broader efforts to strengthen global health security and meet the targets outlined in its Thirteenth Global Programme of Work (2019–2023).
